script: Apparently I could have put the refuse lorry driver in 'fear for his life'. I like cycling, it gives me a sense of peace. I am not in a club, just peddling solo. On the day in question, I was riding a single carriageway that narrowed a bit as it crossed a bridge. I jammed as close to the kerb as I could without rattling my pedals. But here's the thing… the road was about to get a whole lot narrower. A massive "bin" lorry barreled past me, like a freight train in a parking lot. It was huge, the kind that makes you feel like a tiny ant. He swerved right in front of me because he misjudged the speed of an oncoming car. His rear wheel missed my front wheel by about two inches, and I was literally raging. I could have given Eddie Mercury a run for his money if I'd kept my composure. The bin lorry turned left onto a residential street. I followed, pulling up in front of him, ready to unleash my fury. The other workers, who were emptying the bins, watched with interest. I wanted them to see the audacity of the driver's reckless move. What I didn't know was that the driver was about as remorseful as a cat on a hot tin roof. I decided to take action. I reached through the open window, snatched the keys from the ignition, and tossed them into a large bush on the other side of the road. Then I hopped back on my bike and rode away. The wind in my hair felt like a victory lap, but my heart was pounding like a drumbeat. Until… I realized that what I did could land me on a local crime watch show. My partner told me I'd be reported to the police, face legal action, and "put fear for his life" into that heavily built, tattooed, hairy bloke. He was a 5ft 4 slim woman, and I was a 5ft 4 slim female—like, we're both tiny but I am the one who'd get the heat. This wasn't just about a lorry; it was about my own limits. If this didn't work, I'd lose everything—my safety, my peace of mind, my sanity. The stakes were high. I couldn't just walk away. I felt a chill that wasn't just the cold wind. I could hear my own heartbeat in the quiet street. The thought of the police calling my name made my stomach drop to the floor. The guilt started to creep in, like a slow‑motion car crash that you can't see coming. I kept pedaling, but my mind was a battlefield. The loop was open—this was just the beginning of something bigger. I was not just a cyclist; I was a woman who had let anger take the wheel. I couldn't ignore the weight of what I'd done. Imagine your own family doing this to you—no, that's not the point; it's the point that I had a choice, and I chose a path that might end with a ticket. The tension built. The air seemed to thicken, and I could feel the eyes of the workers on me like a spotlight. I thought about the driver's safety, about how my actions could endanger someone. The tension wave hit its peak when I heard the faint hum of a police siren in the distance. That's when everything changed. I pulled over, got off my bike, and called my partner. I confessed everything, the keys, the bush, the fury. My partner's voice was a calm wave in the storm, telling me I was going to get a call from the police. I realized I'd crossed a line that wasn't just a boundary on the road. The loop was closed; the story had a resolution, but the tension lingered like a ghost. I sat on the curb, feeling the weight of my guilt settle. I had to admit that I was wrong. The heat of the moment had blinded me. I could see the driver's truck in the rearview, the way it rattled like a drum. I felt like I had put fear into the heart of a man who had already caused chaos. The moral was clear: anger is a shortcut that leads to regret. In the end, I called the police myself and handed over the keys. The officer took them, apologized, and said we'd do a warning. I was relieved that the worst wasn't happening. I learned that the stakes of a moment can outweigh the thrill of revenge. The final twist? I rode home with a new respect for the road, a lesson in humility, and a story that I'd never repeat. The ride back felt like a quiet victory, and I closed the chapter with a single thought: I am better than the people in the story, but I am still human.
